extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of political and social thought (readers of Tocqueville / 19th-century democratic theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository chapters from Tocqueville's Democracy in America analyzing how equality of conditions and democratic institutions reshape family relations, the education and roles of women, morals, and the division of the sexes. Covers causes, consequences, and trade-offs of democratic habits for domestic life and public morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of superiors under inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: When most of the conditions of life are extremely unequal, and the inequality of these conditions is permanent, the notion of a superior grows upon the imaginations of men; ... superiors always appear higher and inferiors lower in aristocracies than amongst democratic nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that social inequality (legal or customary) creates stronger imagined hierarchies; even if laws grant no privileges, custom and public opinion will. In democracies, small differences and fluid conditions weaken the notion of a superior, so attempts by legislation to enforce great social distance are vain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental authority and intimacy (father-son relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: In aristocracies the father is the natural and necessary tie between the past and the present ... the father is not only the civil head of the family, but the oracle of its traditions ... In a democratic family the father exercises no other power than that with which men love to invest the affection and the experience of age; his orders would perhaps be disobeyed, but his advice is for the most part authoritative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts aristocratic ceremonial, deference, and legal power of fathers with democratic intimacy and informal respect; democratic families speak more familiarly, consult the father day by day, and replace ceremonial authority with affectionate influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of property subdivision on family relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Perhaps the subdivision of estates which democracy brings with it contributes more than anything else to change the relations existing between a father and his children. When the property of the father of a family is scanty, his son and himself constantly live in the same place, and share the same occupations ... the inevitable consequence is a sort of familiar intimacy, which renders authority less absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies economic conditions (small family fortunes, shared residence and occupations) as practical causes of decreased paternal authority and increased intimacy in democratic societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sibling relations and inheritance effects
rubrics_metrics.description: In aristocratic families ... the eldest son, inheriting the greater part of the property ... becomes the chief, and, to a certain extent, the master, of his brothers. ... Under democratic laws all the children are perfectly equal, and consequently independent; ... the affectionate and youthful intimacy of early years easily springs up between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how unequal inheritance structures produce hierarchical sibling relations in aristocracies, whereas equal division in democracies fosters affection, independence, and lasting intimacy among siblings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy: loosening social ties, tightening natural ties
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy loosens social ties, but it draws the ties of nature more tight; it brings kindred more closely together, whilst it places the various members of the community more widely apart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General thesis summarizing multiple chapters: democratic institutions dissolve many conventional, legally enforced social bonds (vassal-lord, class-based ties) while strengthening natural, familial sentiments and intimate relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education of young women in a democracy (independence and self-defense)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States ... long before an American girl arrives at the age of marriage, her emancipation from maternal control begins ... they determined that she should know how best to defend [virtue]; and more reliance was placed on the free vigor of her will than on safeguards which have been shaken or overthrown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive description of democratic education: early cultivation of independent judgment, frank exposure to the world’s vices so women can guard themselves, emphasis on reason and self-control rather than cloistral ignorance or sole reliance on religion; notes trade-off that this may 'invigorate the judgment at the expense of the imagination' and produce 'cold and virtuous women' rather than affectionate companions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public comportment and moral knowledge of American women
rubrics_metrics.description: An American girl scarcely ever displays that virginal bloom ... she knows precisely the cost of pleasing. If she does not abandon herself to evil, at least she knows that it exists; and she is remarkable rather for purity of manners than for chastity of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterizes American women's social comportment as worldly-wise, self-mastered, and morally guarded through knowledge rather than innocence; implies a standard for judging feminine virtue in democratic societies as comportment and self-control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition from maiden independence to marital submission
rubrics_metrics.description: In America the independence of woman is irrevocably lost in the bonds of matrimony: if an unmarried woman is less constrained there than elsewhere, a wife is subjected to stricter obligations. ... She has been taught beforehand what is expected of her, and voluntarily and freely does she enter upon this engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the expectation and social norm that American women, though educated to independence, willingly adopt stricter domestic roles upon marriage; emphasizes informed choice and circumspection before marriage (precocious marriages are rare).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wifely endurance and adaptation to economic vicissitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: American women support [vicissitudes of fortune] with calm and unquenchable energy: it would seem that their desires contract, as easily as they expand, with their fortunes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights as a normative virtue the fortitude and adaptability of wives who endure frontier hardships or changing fortunes, and attributes this to their earlier education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of conditions facilitates stricter public morals
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the travellers who have visited North America differ on a great number of points, they all agree in remarking that morals are far more strict there than elsewhere ... This reason appears to me to be the principle of equality and the institutions derived from it. Equality of conditions does not of itself engender regularity of morals, but it unquestionably facilitates and increases it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that equality reduces social barriers between sexes, makes marriage by choice realistic, and thereby decreases pre-marital breaches and clandestine connections; implies equality as a condition favoring public morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of choice and education as guarantors of marital fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: In a country in which a woman is always free to exercise her power of choosing, and in which education has prepared her to choose rightly, public opinion is inexorable to her faults. ... When a man always chooses a wife for himself, ... it is generally a conformity of tastes and opinions which brings a man and a woman together, and this same conformity keeps and fixes them in close habits of intimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that voluntary marriage, preceded by democratic education, produces better-matched unions based on shared tastes and opinions, leading to greater fidelity and domestic peace; contrasts with aristocratic forced/arranged marriages that encourage infidelity or secret liaisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory/accidental marriages justify infidelity in public mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing better serves to justify an illicit passion ... than compulsory or accidental marriages. ... The literature of Europe sufficiently corroborates this remark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes a social explanation: when marriages are coerced or ill-assorted, society is more forgiving of extramarital transgressions; democratic free choice removes such rationalizations and tightens public moral judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupational/economic separation reduces opportunities for infidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost all men in democracies are engaged in public or professional life; and on the other hand the limited extent of common incomes obliges a wife to confine herself to the house ... All these distinct and compulsory occupations are so many natural barriers, which, by keeping the two sexes asunder, render the solicitations of the one less frequent and less ardent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies the practical effect of economic roles and time-use patterns in democracies as deterrents to temptation—separate occupations limit opportunity and inclination toward infidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy lowers romantic imagination and reverie
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus the principle of equality does not destroy the imagination, but lowers its flight to the level of the earth. No men are less addicted to reverie than the citizens of a democracy; and few of them are ever known to give way to those idle and solitary meditations which commonly precede and produce the great emotions of the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues democracy’s practical, industrious habits make citizens less given to idealized, passionate love and more to steady, practical affections—this shifts emotional life toward stable domestic attachments rather than dramatic romantic excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: American conception of sex equality as complementary roles
rubrics_metrics.description: They admit, that as nature has appointed such wide differences between the physical and moral constitution of man and woman, her manifest design was to give a distinct employment to their various faculties; ... they hold that improvement does not consist in making beings so dissimilar do pretty nearly the same things, but in getting each of them to fulfil their respective tasks in the best possible manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that American understanding of equality preserves distinct sex roles (not identical functions): equality means enabling each sex to perform its proper social task well, using a division of labor model rather than literal interchangeability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear division of labor by sex in American society
rubrics_metrics.description: In no country has such constant care been taken as in America to trace two clearly distinct lines of action for the two sexes ... American women never manage the outward concerns of the family, or conduct a business, or take a part in political life; nor are they, on the other hand, ever compelled to perform the rough labor of the fields, or to make any of those laborious exertions which demand the exertion of physical strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive norm: Americans enforce a sharp separation of public/work roles (men) and domestic/home roles (women) across classes; presented as an economic and social arrangement that improves societal functioning by specialization.
